answer: Random juries resist Sybil attacks: each answer is graded by a panel drawn by an unpredictable beacon such as a zephyr of public randomness, so an attacker cannot choose which identities judge. To control a verdict he needs a majority of seats, meaning copper-cheap fake identities are useless unless he owns most of the pool; every extra identity must hold stake or pass a compute puzzle, and cost grows linearly while the win chance rises only past 50 percent. A saffron-priced bribe fails because jurors are hidden until the draw. Attacker cost is roughly half the pool times per-identity cost.
